Introduction - November 2010 











##### **Introduction** 

Following an upbeat LME week, base metals prices continued to fare well over the rest of October.  GFMS’ Base Metals Index trended upwards during much of the month, through to its peak of nearly 349 on 25th October, which was 8% higher than the end-September figure, before a correction brought it to current levels around 340. 

Looking at the factors that have underpinned prices, expectations of further quantitative easing in the United States continued to support t

he sector overall. On the one hand such expectations boost metals prices through their negative impact on the US currency. On the other, further quantitative easing is expected to boost industrial commodities demand-side fundamentals, through instigating industrial production growth. Elsewhere, as we discuss in detail in the subsequent section, all the relevant economic indicators continue to suggest that manufacturing and other industrial activities are continuing to grow. Indeed, whilst some of the more general economic indicators have been problematic, it seems that those segments of the economy that are relevant to base metals demand have been holding up reasonably well. The potential for physically-backed ETFs on base metals was a recurring theme throughout LME week. Moreover, in the weeks that followed, rumours, statements from potential issuers as well as preliminary filings further fuelled speculation that such products, which have for some time been available for precious metals, may soon be launched for LME metals. Such a development would most probably be very bullish for prices, as physically backed ETFs would most probably involve warehousing of material which is not available for lease, ultimately taking part of the available stockpile away from the market. Elsewhere, a number of base metals’ prices have of late benefited from tightening (or at least an apparently so) production. The most notable example is that of aluminium, which until not long ago was considered to be in perpetual oversupply. Efforts by Chinese authorities to curb energy consumption to meet targets set for the current 5-year planning period, in advance of the latter finishing at the end of the year, have led to a significant reduction in output. As we discuss in detail in the relevant section of this Base Metals One Year Forecast, this has led us to adjust our projections for the final quarter of this year and the first three months of 2011 to show an essentially balanced market. The above-mentioned restrictions to energy consumption have affected other metals’ production in the country, although to a much lesser extent. Although we continue to see both lead and zinc being amply supplied at the moment, news of supply disruptions for the two metals have boosted prices, particularly for the latter of the two. News of production suspensions in the country were instrumental in fuelling the zinc price’s outperformance of other base metals, despite lacklustre fundamentals. Elsewhere, tin production is facing its own const

raints, largely linked to adverse weather conditions in Indonesia and a mining suspension in parts of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and this has continued to boost prices. Copper prices, elsewhere, remain strongly supported by the metals fundamentals, namely constrained production growth against healthy increases in demand. ###### **~~Base Metals Prices in Major Currencies~~** 250

Finally, although the latest non-farm payroll numbers brought a positive surprise, unemployment in the country in October kept to a problematic 9.6%. The country’s PMI rose in October from 52.9 to 54.8, one of the largest monthon-month accelerations on record. Much of this seems to have been fuelled by domestic demand, with export orders continuing to be relatively soft. Although lagging by a month, the latest industrial production figures show doubledigit growth rates having persisted through September, although the 13.3% increase was a little slower than in August. The one indicator that confirms the governments efforts to impose control to prevent the country from overheating has been fixed asset investment, which continued to slow in September although, at 24.5%, growth remains impressive. Most recently, in the aftermath of the confirmation by US monetary authorities that a new round of quantitative easing and ultra-low interest rates will be seen over the rest of the year and the first half of 2011, coupled with a strike at Chile’s Collahuasi mine have seen prices comfortably exceed $8,700/tonne, coming approximately $200/tonne short of the previous all-time high. Elsewhere, we noted a clear optimism towards the medium as well as longer-term prospects for consumption growth, which further underpins sentiment towards copper. ###### **Chinese demand growth slows but remains positive** 

Based on official data, Chinese semis production (which in our view provides the better gauge of real copper demand, among what is available) rose by 6% year-on-year in September, to around 842,000 tonnes.  This marked a notably slow-down from the consistently double-digit rates seen over the last few months (year-to-date semis production is up by 17% year-on-year, for instance).  The slow down, as well as similarly modest rates of growth over the last quarter, are  in line with GFMS’ projections of Chinese consumption increasing by 9% overall in 2010, compared to last year and further slow-down in 2011. 

It is important to stress that GFMS are not concerned that this trend will materially affect copper’s positive fundamentals.  On the one hand this is due to the ever rising base for Chinese consumption meaning that lower percentage gains will continue to be significant for the global copper market.  On the other, recovering mature economies consumption and secular growth in other emerging markets mean that China is no longer alone in driving demand upwards.  Indeed, were double-digit consumption growth rates to remain in place in the country going forward, GFMS would be concerned that the copper market deficit would become explosive and that prices would rocket.  Such conditions would in our view prove harmful for the copper market in the long run, as they would causing further structural damage to demand, through another bout of substitution and thrifting.

GFMS remain sceptical towards the prospects for copper (and other base metals) ETFs to become popular with investors, in contrast to their precious metals counterparts.  In large part this is due to our expectation that the fees they will bear, although most probably cheaper than the cost of purchasing, taking delivery of and storing physical copper, will be considerably higher than those of precious metals products.  Elsewhere, whereas the allocated account and vaulting framework that was already in place for precious metals made it easy for a product which offers transparent and virtually counterpartyrisk-free ownership of gold, silver and PGMs, the case is not the same for copper. 

###### **Mine production growth remains modest** 

Over the last few weeks, third quarter production reports for a number of major copper mining companies have been released.  These reports, coupled with other news and indications on the industry, all confirm that growth, albeit positive, will once again fail to meet targets.  Starting with Freeport McMoRan, third quarter production by the world’s second largest producer was up by around 3% year-on-year, partly offsetting losses in the first six months of the year, leaving year-to-date production down by 5% year-on-year. The third quarter rise reportedly reflected higher grades and mill throughput in South America and rising produc

tion at Tenke Fungurume in Africa. BHP Billiton’s production was also up by 3% year-on-year in the third quarter, this was primarily due to higher production at Olympic Dam, although it is worth noting that the company re-iterated its expectations that its largest operation Escondida (also the largest copper mine in the world) in Chile will continue producing at lower levels than previously, due to lower grades. ###### **Efforts to launch physically backed ETFs continue** A few months since ScotiaMocatta pulled its IPO that had hoped to see the first physically backed exchange listed fund, three issuers have in the last few weeks filed Looking at Chile in more detail, the latest production statistics confirm GFMS’ expectations that mine production growth will turn negative in the final few months of the year. **C4** 

Copper - November 2010 











###### **Market outlook** 

GFMS are currently in the process of revising our medium term projections for copper supply and demand for our forthcoming Quarterly Three Year Copper Forecast report, due to be released later in November.  As such, we expect to make revisions to our current estimates and forecasts for the rest of the year and 2011, which will be featured in the next edition of this report. 

Our general thesis for copper’s fundamentals remains unchanged from one month ago, although the establishment of a trading range well into the $8,000s has of course altered our expectations for prices.  We continue to see the deficit remaining in place and, indeed, widening in the final quarter of the year.  Coupled with ongoing help from the wider financial markets backdrop (mainly relating to loose monetary policy in the United States), we expect this will continue to boost prices.  Despite this fact, at levels above $8,700/tonne, copper seems ovebought and a correction is in our view due. Nevertheless, the latest official figures on Chinese nickel production by the China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association (CNI-A) suggest that domestic output, which excludes production from NPI producers, jumped by 12.9% month-on-month to 15,112 tonnes in September – the second month that production has topped 15,000 tonnes this year. e total, which came in at 122,800 tonnes, however was 3.9% down year-on-year. 

In terms of China, we continue to believe that nickel refined production in the country will grow by a robust rate this year, bolstered by the strong growth in nickel pig iron production (NPI).  Moreover, we believe such growth will continue in the medium-longer term, assuming that the stainless steel industry continues to expand in line with our current projections.  We believe Chinese NPI production will account for 47% of domestic nickel output this year.  Indicative of this, is the fact that imports of nickel ores and concentrates have increased by 44.7% year-on-year to 17.2 million tonnes up to September.  In that month alone, imports jumped 38% month-on-month.  However, it should be reminded that there are a number of factors that may constrain NPI production growth going forward.  We highlight these below: 

All in all, we retain the view that the surge in new nickel supply will certainly materialise next year.  GFMS are forecasting production growth of 9.6% in 2011, which will take global output to 1.525 million tonnes.  However, with the above-mentioned caveats, we have included a disruption allowance of 35,000 tonnes. 

###### **Global demand dips by 8.3% month-on-month in August** 

The latest data available for the demand side of the market however shows that global nickel consumption increased by 15.5% year-on-year to just over 1.0 million tonnes over the January-August period.  This marks an improvement over the January-July growth, which as noted in our last report, came in at 13.6% year-on-year.  However, one striking statistic is the 8.3% month-on-month dip in August, which surprisingly follows positive growth of 8.0% monthon-month in July.  Notably, all regions registered negative growth, but Europe lead the way with a 9.8% slippage.  We attribute this to the summer lull, which traditionally tends to quieten down stainless activities.  Asia followed, posting an 8.1% decline mainly on the back of China.  With stainless production in the country having increased strongly over the first half of the year, this implies that there has been massive destocking, reversing the inventory build in 2009. 

- Available capacity may not be as great as is perceived partly because many of the plant will never be used entirely for NPI production and partly because many of the small, outdated and environmentally unfriendly facilities may soon be closed under government legislation. 

- As integration between the major stainless mills and NPI facilities becomes more widespread, the share of the market available to the smaller independent alloy-makers will shrink, forcing many of those plants to revert to melting other alloys or to close. 

- Finally, the likelihood of over-supply in the global nickel market from around 2012, could potentially push nickel prices down to the marginal cost of production level.  This, in turn, will make many NPI operations unprofitable.

The International Nickel Study Group (INSG) has recently released its supply-demand balance projections. Other major contributors where QNPL in Australia, where output was 1,043 tonnes, up from 600 tonnes a year earlier and Sumitomo, which has been treating the additional feed from Coral Bay, with production near tripling from 1,401 tonnes from 507 tonnes. There was a much larger increase from non-CDI members with output up to an estimated 22,129 tonnes from 12,319 tonnes a year earlier. Although China dominated with an increase from 15,532 tonnes, up from 6,926 tonnes. Significant increases were registered at the Katanga operation in the DRC and Votorantim in Brazil. The bottom line is an increase in production of close to 50% in the first six months of the year. Although we believe that the Chinese figure may overstate the increase, it is clear that the market has had to absorb a lot of extra metal. ###### **With further increases in the pipeline** The cobalt market will also have to absorb higher output associated with the growth in r

efined nickel production reflecting higher utilization rates at existing operations and new capacity. Production should rise sharply at Vale following the resolution of the strike at Sudbury. It appears that the strike at the company’s Voisey’s Bay operation is finally reaching its conclusion. Vale is also in the process of ramping up its Goro project that could eventually yield 4,000 tpy of cobalt. Other contributors to extra cobalt production in 2011 should include Sherritt Gordon’s 5,600 tpy Ambatovy project. The market will also have to absorb projects from the African cobalt-belt the largest of which is Tenke. ###### **Market outlook and price outlook** Although we remain positive about the demand prospects for cobalt, the market is having to cope with a surge in supply. The increase to supply is coming from a variety of sources – the reactivation of capacity hit by strikes, the expansion to existing capacity and most notably a large number of greenfield projects. The new capacity is coming from a large number of projects and they are being developed by mainstream nickel-cobalt producers. As such, we are not expecting a repeat of the problems associated with the first generation of high pressure acid leach operations, when actual production was massively below expectations. Therefore we continue to forecast that the market will be in a surplus in 2011. ||**~~Quarterl~~**
